indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.1.1. Demonstrate knowledge of the ethnic groups in Ghana
indicator.objective: Identify the ethnic groups in each region in Ghana

skills.description: Tell the name of a region from the name of a people.
Match named groups with regions using examples.
Use a map key or caption to locate an ethnic group.
Use local accounts and records to identify groups fairly.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: A town, a region and a people can have different names.
A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.
A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.
Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

questions.stem: Three map cards say “Kumasi city”, “Ashanti Region” and “Asante people”. Which name belongs on a list of regions?
hints: Read the kind of place or people named on each card.
questions.explanation: Ashanti is a region. Asante is the name of a people with deep roots there.
questions.misconception: A town, a region and a people can have different names.

distractorMisconceptions.Kumasi: Kumasi is a city in Ashanti.
distractorMisconceptions.Ghana: Ghana is the country that contains the regions.

questions.stem: A class card reads “Ga people, Greater Accra Region”. Copy the name of the people.
hints: Find the word just before “people”.
questions.explanation: Ga names the people. Greater Accra names a region where many Ga people live.
questions.misconception: A town, a region and a people can have different names.

questions.stem: Say which is the region and which is the group in “many Fante people live in Central Region”.
hints: Listen to the words that follow each name.
questions.explanation: Fante names a people. Central Region is one place where many Fante families live.
questions.misconception: A town, a region and a people can have different names.

criteria.description: Names Fante as the group.
Names Central as the region.

questions.stem: Your class map shows an Anlo Ewe community in Volta Region. Make one label for the region and one for the community.
hints: One label describes the area and the other names people.
questions.explanation: The area label can read Volta. A second label can show an example such as Anlo Ewe.
questions.misconception: A town, a region and a people can have different names.

criteria.description: Labels the area Volta Region.
Adds an accurately identified group, such as Anlo Ewe.

questions.stem: A pupil says that every child in the Ashanti Region must be Asante. What could you say? Give an example.
hints: Think of families who move to a new town.
questions.explanation: Many Asante people live in Ashanti. A Ga family can also make its home there.
questions.misconception: A town, a region and a people can have different names.

criteria.description: Explains that several ethnic groups can live in a region.
Gives a possible example without guessing a classmate’s ethnicity.

questions.stem: A map note says that Dagomba communities live around Yendi in Northern Region. Which pair gives the people and their region?
hints: Use the words that come before “communities” and before “Region”.
questions.explanation: The Dagomba people of Dagbon have long lived in what is now the Northern Region.
questions.misconception: A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.

distractorMisconceptions.Dagbon — Yendi: Dagbon is a kingdom and Yendi is a town. The answer needs a people and a region.
distractorMisconceptions.Yendi — Dagomba: Yendi names a town and Dagomba names a people.
distractorMisconceptions.Northern — Yendi: This pairs a region with a town.

questions.stem: A card shows “Sefwi — Western North” and “Nzema — Western”. Where should the Sefwi label go?
hints: Follow the full name on the Sefwi card.
questions.explanation: Western North is the region on the Sefwi card. Western is a separate region on this map.
questions.misconception: A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.

distractorMisconceptions.Western Region: This is the region on the Nzema card.
distractorMisconceptions.Northern Region: Northern is a different region from Western North.
distractorMisconceptions.North East Region: Sharing the word North does not make the names alike.

questions.stem: Match the first name to the second in each pair: “Kwahu — Eastern” and “Bono — Bono”. What does each pair tell us?
hints: Use a sentence that says who lives where.
questions.explanation: Many Kwahu people live in Eastern Region. Bono communities live in Bono Region, where the people and the region share a name.
questions.misconception: A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.

criteria.description: States the correct Eastern Region example.
States the correct Bono Region example.

questions.stem: Your class key shows Akan communities in Ahafo and Bono East, and Guan communities in Oti. Make a label for each of the three regions and read your labels to a partner.
hints: More than one place can share a group label.
questions.explanation: Akan communities live in both Ahafo and Bono East. Guan communities are among the people who live in Oti.
questions.misconception: A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.

criteria.description: Places Akan community labels in both named regions.
Pairs Guan communities with Oti and reads the labels correctly.

questions.stem: Kofi puts “Gonja” in a box called “a region”. His two cards say “Gonja people” and “Savannah Region”. Rewrite the labels and explain your change.
hints: What does each name tell a map reader?
questions.explanation: One box can say “People: Gonja”. The other can say “Region: Savannah”. The pair names a people and a place where many live.
questions.misconception: A group can have roots in a region and also live elsewhere.

criteria.description: Places both names in their proper boxes.
Explains why the labels mean different things.

questions.stem: Which part of a map tells what its coloured dots mean?
hints: Look for the part that explains symbols.
questions.explanation: The key lists the symbols and their meanings. It tells you which group each dot stands for.
questions.misconception: A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.

distractorMisconceptions.The date: The date says when the map was made.
distractorMisconceptions.The title: The title names the topic of the whole map.

questions.stem: Your map key says a triangle means Mamprusi people. You see a triangle in North East Region. Which people does it mark?
hints: Read the symbol before you read the place name.
questions.explanation: The triangle means Mamprusi. The triangle’s place on this map gives an example of a Mamprusi community in North East Region.
questions.misconception: A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.

questions.stem: A star marks a Dagaaba community in Upper West. A circle marks a Frafra community in Upper East. Which label belongs beside the circle?
hints: Find the sentence that tells what the circle means.
questions.explanation: The circle is the Frafra example in Upper East. The star belongs to the other example.
questions.misconception: A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.

distractorMisconceptions.Dagaaba in Upper East: This keeps the circle’s region but takes the star’s group.
distractorMisconceptions.Frafra in Upper West: This keeps the circle’s group but takes the star’s region.
distractorMisconceptions.Dagaaba in Upper West: This is the label for the star.

questions.stem: Use paper circles for two Ewe communities, one in Volta and one in Greater Accra. Make a key so a friend can read your map.
hints: Use the same symbol for both communities.
questions.explanation: Two circles can mark two communities in different regions. One key can explain both circles.
questions.misconception: A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.

criteria.description: Places one circle under each correct region label.
Makes a key that identifies both circles as Ewe communities.

questions.stem: A map has no key. A pupil says a blue dot in Oti must mean a Guan community. What would you check before agreeing?
hints: Find out who chose that colour and what it stands for.
questions.explanation: Guan communities live in Oti, but a blue dot could mean something else. The maker’s key or caption would tell you.
questions.misconception: A map symbol gets its meaning from the key.

criteria.description: Explains why the dot alone is not enough.
Names a suitable source for the meaning of the dot.

questions.stem: Which class question could help find out about groups in a town?
hints: Choose a question about people and their communities.
questions.explanation: Asking community members which groups have homes there can lead to names that the class can check.
questions.misconception: Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

distractorMisconceptions.Which road is longest?: Road length does not identify a group.
distractorMisconceptions.Which roof is highest?: A building's height does not tell who lives in the town.
distractorMisconceptions.Which bus is fastest?: Travel speed does not name any group.

questions.stem: A town guide says, “Many Ga and Dangme families live in Greater Accra.” Which group name comes after Ga?
hints: Follow the two names joined by “and”.
questions.explanation: The guide names Ga and Dangme families. Dangme is the second group named.
questions.misconception: Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

questions.stem: A neighbour tells you the name of a group that lives in your region. Ask a polite question to learn where to put it on a map.
hints: Try asking about the town or part of the region.
questions.explanation: Asking “Which town has a community you know about?” gives the class a place for its map label.
questions.misconception: Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

criteria.description: Poses a respectful question.
Asks for a location connected to the group.

questions.stem: A guide says that Ga and Ewe families live in one town. Draw the town as one box. Add labels that keep both groups on your map.
hints: There can be two labels inside one boundary.
questions.explanation: A single town box can contain both Ga and Ewe labels. A boundary does not divide people automatically.
questions.misconception: Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

criteria.description: Represents one town.
Places both group names within it.

questions.stem: Your class has heard from just one family about one region. What can you put on your display now, and how can you add other groups later?
hints: Separate the example you have from the ones you still need.
questions.explanation: Name the community the family described. Then ask other people or check a map with a key before adding more labels.
questions.misconception: Clothes, names or appearances alone do not establish a person's ethnic group.

criteria.description: Describes one supported entry for the display.
Identifies a reasonable way to check an additional group.

uncertain: Printed page 10 gives the same indicator code to the region-matching and characteristics objectives.
The curriculum does not list regional matches or dates of creation. Map exercises give their own keys and do not score an unsupported sequence of regions.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.1.1. Show understanding of the characteristics of some of the ethnic groups in Ghana
indicator.objective: State the characteristics of the ethnic groups in Ghana

skills.description: Connect festivals to communities and the events they remember.
Identify examples of food and dress and the skills behind them.
Recognise language and leadership as aspects of community life.
Describe what a source shows and make fair comparisons.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.
Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.
One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.
A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

questions.stem: A Ga festival poster reads “Homowo: remembering how our people overcame hunger”. Which word gives the festival’s name?
hints: Look for the name at the head of the poster.
questions.explanation: Homowo remembers hunger in the past and the good harvest that followed.
questions.misconception: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.

distractorMisconceptions.Harvest: A harvest is an event in the story.
distractorMisconceptions.Festival: Festival names a kind of celebration.

questions.stem: Anlo families celebrate Hogbetsotso. Copy the name of their festival.
hints: Find the word naming the celebration.
questions.explanation: Hogbetsotso is the festival. Anlo is the name of the community in this sentence.
questions.misconception: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.

questions.stem: A guide says Hogbetsotso remembers a journey by Anlo ancestors. Tell a friend whose story it is and what it remembers.
hints: Think of who travelled long ago.
questions.explanation: The story belongs to the Anlo community. The festival remembers their ancestors' journey away from Notsie.
questions.misconception: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.

criteria.description: Names the Anlo or Anlo Ewe community.
Describes the memory of the ancestors' journey.

questions.stem: A Ga speaker says, “At Homowo we remember hunger and the harvest that followed.” Make a poster about what the speaker remembers.
hints: You might use a picture of food or a harvest.
questions.explanation: A drawing of a good harvest can tell how Ga people remember overcoming hunger.
questions.misconception: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.

criteria.description: Adds a feature linked to Homowo.
Explains its connection to the memory of overcoming hunger.

questions.stem: A Ga speaker links Homowo to surviving hunger. An Anlo speaker links Hogbetsotso to a journey. A display calls both “a harvest story”. Fix the captions using what each speaker said.
hints: One story is about hunger and harvest. The other is about a journey.
questions.explanation: Homowo recalls the Ga people's experience of hunger and harvest. Hogbetsotso recalls the journey of Anlo ancestors.
questions.misconception: A festival can tell a story about the past as well as bring people together.

criteria.description: Correctly matches Homowo to the Ga memory.
Correctly matches Hogbetsotso to the Anlo memory.

questions.stem: A weaver shows the class strips of kente and says she will join them to make something to wear. Which item will the strips become?
hints: Think about where a person might wear the finished work.
questions.explanation: A weaver joins woven strips into cloth. Kente can be worn at special occasions.
questions.misconception: Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.

distractorMisconceptions.A clay pot: Clay pots are shaped from clay.
distractorMisconceptions.A wooden stool: A wooden stool is carved or built from wood.

questions.stem: Kpokpoi is a maize dish served at Homowo. Which heading fits this example?
hints: Decide what can be eaten.
questions.explanation: A maize dish is food. A festival can include different kinds of cultural activity.
questions.misconception: Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.

distractorMisconceptions.Festival music: A dish is eaten rather than played.
distractorMisconceptions.Festival language: A dish's name is a word but the dish itself is food.

questions.stem: Sort these words into food and dress: kpokpoi, a woven kente wrap. Explain one choice.
hints: Ask what a person does with each item.
questions.explanation: Kpokpoi goes under food because it is eaten. A kente wrap goes under dress because it is worn.
questions.misconception: Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.

criteria.description: Places both items in suitable groups.
Gives a reason for one placement.

questions.stem: Draw threads, a woven strip and a finished cloth. Point to the part made by weaving and describe it.
hints: Follow the work a weaver does at a loom.
questions.explanation: The weaver crosses threads to form a strip. Strips can then be joined to make the cloth.
questions.misconception: Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.

criteria.description: Shows woven strips as part of the cloth.
Explains what the weaver does.

questions.stem: An Asante weaver and an Ewe weaver both make kente. A friend thinks one has the wrong job. Explain what both examples show.
hints: Can a craft belong to more than one tradition?
questions.explanation: Both communities have traditions of weaving kente. Seeing the cloth alone cannot tell us a person's ethnic group.
questions.misconception: Foods and cloth can be shared by people of several backgrounds.

criteria.description: Recognises both traditions as valid.
Explains that sharing a craft does not make the groups identical.

questions.stem: A visitor teaches the class a greeting in Ewe. What part of community life is the class learning about?
hints: Think about the words people use to speak.
questions.explanation: A greeting uses words from a language. In this example the language is Ewe.
questions.misconception: One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.

questions.stem: “The Dagomba speak Dagbani” is on a class card. Which word names the language?
hints: Look for what the people speak.
questions.explanation: Dagbani names a language spoken by Dagomba people. Dagomba names the people.
questions.misconception: One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.

questions.stem: A film shows a chief and elders hearing a village matter. Which heading fits that scene best?
hints: Think about the job they are doing in this scene.
questions.explanation: The chief and elders are helping guide the community. The scene shows traditional leadership.
questions.misconception: One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.

distractorMisconceptions.Traditional dress: The question asks about their work, even if their dress is visible.
distractorMisconceptions.Traditional food: There is no meal in the scene.
distractorMisconceptions.Traditional games: This is a community matter rather than a game.

questions.stem: Abena speaks Twi with her aunt and Ga with a friend. What two things can her example teach us about language?
hints: Count the languages she uses and notice whom she talks to.
questions.explanation: Abena uses two languages. A person can use different languages with different people.
questions.misconception: One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.

criteria.description: Names the two languages in the example.
Explains that one person can use more than one language.

questions.stem: Make a card for the heading “community life”. On it, name a language or a leader you know about and tell how the example fits.
hints: Choose a name you have heard in a lesson or from a community member.
questions.explanation: A card might name Dagbani and say that people use it to talk to one another. A card about a leader might explain a duty.
questions.misconception: One example of a language or leader does not describe every person.

criteria.description: Gives a specific and accurate example of language or leadership.
Tells how the example is part of a community's life.

questions.stem: Which note says what a pupil can actually see in a festival picture?
hints: Choose a detail that a camera can show.
questions.explanation: The picture can show two people playing drums. It cannot show what every family does each day.
questions.misconception: A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

A picture of players cannot show everyone’s belongings.
One picture cannot show its length.
The picture gives no evidence about every family.

questions.stem: A film note says “we hear Ewe songs and see a dance”. Which word in the note names a language?
hints: Read the word that tells which songs the class hears.
questions.explanation: The note identifies Ewe as the language of the songs. It also names a dance but gives no name for the dance.
questions.misconception: A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

questions.stem: At a festival, a visitor sees a special cloth for the first time. Ask its wearer a polite question about it.
hints: Ask about something you would like to understand.
questions.explanation: “Would you tell me when you wear this cloth?” lets the wearer explain its use in their own words.
questions.misconception: A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

criteria.description: Asks respectfully about the cloth.
Leaves room for the wearer to describe their own experience.

questions.stem: One class picture shows a family sharing food. Another shows a family singing. Draw a label for each and tell one difference.
hints: Look closely at the actions.
questions.explanation: The first label can show a dish. The other can show a song. These actions show different parts of a celebration.
questions.misconception: A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

criteria.description: Distinguishes sharing food from singing.
Connects both labels to the scenes in the question.

questions.stem: A visitor watches one family prepare a festival meal and writes “everyone eats this every day”. Give a better sentence and a question to ask.
hints: What did the visitor see on that one day?
questions.explanation: “This family made this meal for the festival” fits what was seen. Asking when else they eat it would help the visitor learn more.
questions.misconception: A short film or photograph shows one example, not every family's habits.

criteria.description: Replaces the claim with a statement limited to the observed family and occasion.
Asks a relevant question about the practice.

uncertain: Printed page 10 repeats the preceding indicator code for this separate objective.
Printed page 10 gives categories of cultural characteristics but no named festival accounts. Tasks provide descriptions or invite a teacher-checked local example.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.4.1. Exhibit knowledge of the history of the major historical locations in Ghana
indicator.objective: Discuss the history of Ghana’s major historical locations. Examples include Kumasi military museum, Komfo Anokye Sword, Assin Manso slave site, Gbewa Palace.

skills.description: Identify historical places by name and location.
Connect each site with the people and past it helps us remember.
Use objects, signs and accounts to learn a site's story.
Retell and compare the histories of sites using clear details.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: A town may contain more than one historical site.
A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.
An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.
Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.

questions.stem: A class map marks the Komfo Anokye Sword Site in Kumasi. Which town should appear on the class trip card?
hints: Use the place named on the map.
questions.explanation: The sword site is in Kumasi. Visitors go there to learn about an Asante tradition.
questions.misconception: A town may contain more than one historical site.

distractorMisconceptions.Yendi: Yendi is associated with Gbewaa Palace.
distractorMisconceptions.Assin Manso: Assin Manso has a different historical site by a river.
distractorMisconceptions.Elmina: Elmina's well-known castle is on the coast.

questions.stem: A sign reads “Gbewaa Palace, Yendi”. What town does the sign name?
hints: Find the place named after the comma.
questions.explanation: Gbewaa Palace is the site. Yendi is the town.
questions.misconception: A town may contain more than one historical site.

questions.stem: A guide names two Kumasi stops: the Military Museum and the Komfo Anokye Sword Site. Tell what each stop is called and which one is about the sword.
hints: Think of a museum and a separate site.
questions.explanation: The military museum and the Komfo Anokye Sword Site are both in Kumasi. The sword site is the place linked to the sword tradition.
questions.misconception: A town may contain more than one historical site.

criteria.description: Names the military museum and sword site.
Identifies the sword site as the place linked to Komfo Anokye.

questions.stem: A guide's card says “Gbewaa Palace in Yendi is linked to the Yaa Naa of Dagbon”. Draw a direction card using the site and town.
hints: Think of the palace associated with the Yaa Naa.
questions.explanation: The card can name Gbewaa Palace and Yendi. These two names tell a visitor what place to ask for and where.
questions.misconception: A town may contain more than one historical site.

criteria.description: Identifies Gbewaa or Gbewa Palace.
Identifies Yendi as the town.

questions.stem: A trip card says “Kumasi” and nothing else. Your friend needs to find the military museum there. How would you improve the card, and why?
hints: Think of two sites in that city.
questions.explanation: Add “Kumasi Fort and Military Museum”. A town name alone could send a visitor to another site, such as the sword site.
questions.misconception: A town may contain more than one historical site.

criteria.description: Adds a name that identifies the military museum.
Explains why the town alone leaves a choice of sites.

questions.stem: What can the Kumasi Military Museum help a class learn about?
hints: Think about the word military in its name.
questions.explanation: The museum keeps objects and records about soldiers and military history.
questions.misconception: A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.

distractorMisconceptions.The growth of cocoa: Farming is not the subject named here.
distractorMisconceptions.The work of weavers: Cloth making is a different subject.
distractorMisconceptions.The growth of fishing: Fishing is not the subject named here.

questions.stem: Which site helps us remember people taken from their homes and sold during the slave trade?
hints: Think of the river site studied in class.
questions.explanation: At Assin Manso people were held and sold against their will. Remembering them is part of the history of the site.
questions.misconception: A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.

distractorMisconceptions.Gbewaa Palace: The palace is associated with the rulers of Dagbon.
distractorMisconceptions.Komfo Anokye Sword Site: The sword site is linked to an Asante tradition.
distractorMisconceptions.Kumasi Military Museum: The named museum focuses on military history.

questions.stem: A guide says, “This was a fort before it became the Kumasi Military Museum.” Retell the change in your own words.
hints: What was the older building used as, and what can visitors do there now?
questions.explanation: The building was once a fort. Later it became a museum where people can learn about the past.
questions.misconception: A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.

criteria.description: Puts the fort before the museum.
Describes the museum's later role.

questions.stem: A guide says, “Gbewaa Palace is linked with the Yaa Naa, king of Dagbon.” Make a picture caption that identifies the kingdom and the ruler.
hints: Think of the royal title in Dagbon.
questions.explanation: The palace is connected to the rulers of Dagbon. The Yaa Naa is the king of Dagbon.
questions.misconception: A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.

criteria.description: Connects the palace with Dagbon.
Connects it to the Yaa Naa or the kings of Dagbon.

questions.stem: Someone says the site at Assin Manso is only a river. Tell one thing about its past and why visitors remember the people there.
hints: Think of the difference between a river and the story of the people taken there.
questions.explanation: Enslaved people were brought to the site by force. People visit today to remember their lives and what happened to them.
questions.misconception: A site’s story can matter even when the place has a new use.

criteria.description: Mentions forced captivity or sale in the history of the site.
Gives a respectful reason to remember the people.

questions.stem: Which item would best help a visitor learn what an old uniform in a museum was used for?
hints: Look for words that belong to that display.
questions.explanation: The label beside the uniform may name who wore it and what it was used for.
questions.misconception: An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.

distractorMisconceptions.A visitor's ticket price: The price helps people enter the museum.
distractorMisconceptions.The shop's opening time: Opening time tells when a shop opens.
distractorMisconceptions.A bus route number: A bus route helps a visitor travel.

questions.stem: At a site, Esi reads this label: “This drum was used to call people to meetings.” What object does the label describe?
hints: Look for the thing that made the sound.
questions.explanation: The label names a drum and explains its use. The object and its label give two connected clues.
questions.misconception: An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.

questions.stem: A guide begins, “One story told by elders about the sword is …”. How should you begin when you retell it?
hints: Keep the guide's clue about where the account comes from.
questions.explanation: Saying that elders tell the story keeps the source with the account. Hearing a story does not make the listener an eyewitness.
questions.misconception: An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.

distractorMisconceptions.“I saw it happen long ago …”: Hearing the guide is different from seeing the original event.
distractorMisconceptions.“The ticket price proves that …”: A price gives no evidence about the tradition.
distractorMisconceptions.“The gate colour proves that …”: A gate's colour cannot establish the story.

questions.stem: Pretend a partner is a guide at a historical site. Ask about one object, then tell the class what your partner reported.
hints: Start with a question about how people used it.
questions.explanation: A pupil might ask how a drum was used and report the guide's reply that it called people to meetings.
questions.misconception: An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.

criteria.description: Asks a relevant question about an object.
Reports the answer accurately and identifies the guide as the source.

questions.stem: A photo shows the outside of a palace. Give one detail the photo could show and one question you would still ask about its past.
hints: Look at what a camera can catch from outside.
questions.explanation: A photo can show a gate. A guide or local account could explain who used that gate and why.
questions.misconception: An object without a label or source cannot tell its full history.

criteria.description: Names a visible feature the photo could show.
Asks a historical question that needs further evidence.

questions.stem: Which question asks about the history of a place?
hints: Look for a question about what happened there.
questions.explanation: Asking who gathered there long ago can reveal past activity at the site.
questions.misconception: Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.
options: How bright is the sun today?
Where can we put our lunch?

distractorMisconceptions.How bright is the sun today?: Today's light is not about the site's past.
distractorMisconceptions.Where can we put our lunch?: That question is about the present visit.
distractorMisconceptions.Which seat is free today?: The seat question is about today's arrangements.

questions.stem: A class display says “Assin Manso remembers people who were enslaved.” Copy the name of the place on this display.
hints: Find the name before “remembers”.
questions.explanation: Assin Manso is the place named. The rest of the caption tells whose history it helps visitors remember.
questions.misconception: Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.

questions.stem: Tell a short story about a historical site in your community or one from class. Begin with its name and say what happened there.
hints: Pick one place you can link to people in the past.
questions.explanation: For example, Kumasi Fort was used as a fort before people turned it into a military museum.
questions.misconception: Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.

criteria.description: Identifies a real site.
Accurately connects the site with a past event, use or tradition.

questions.stem: A visitor saw soldiers' uniforms at the Kumasi Military Museum and heard about the rulers of Dagbon at Gbewaa Palace. Draw a sign for each place and explain your symbols.
hints: Choose a different symbol to show the story told at each site.
questions.explanation: A uniform could stand for the military museum. A palace entrance could lead into the story of Dagbon's rulers.
questions.misconception: Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.

criteria.description: Uses distinct symbols or captions for the sites.
Explains a relevant historical connection for each.

questions.stem: A postcard says only “We saw a river and a museum.” Add the two site names and one fact about each so another class can learn from it.
hints: Use the river site at Assin Manso and the military museum in Kumasi.
questions.explanation: The river site at Assin Manso remembers people who were enslaved. The museum in Kumasi keeps objects that tell of soldiers' lives.
questions.misconception: Naming a site or describing its appearance alone does not retell its history.

criteria.description: Correctly links the named river site to its history.
Correctly links the named museum to its history.

uncertain: The class section names sites but does not give dates or a sequence by age. Activities use brief guide accounts and ask children to identify what those accounts show.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B2.2.5.1.1 Exhibit understanding of Ghanaian women who have contributed significantly to Ghana’s development
indicator.objective: Identify Ghanaian women who have made significant contributions to national development

skills.description: Match Ghanaian women with their achievements.
Tell how women led the work of Ghana's courts and Parliament.
Explain how a woman's work helped people or opened opportunities.
Use details about real women to explain admiration and contribution.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.
The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.
A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.
Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.

questions.stem: Which Ghanaian woman became a pilot?
hints: Think about someone whose work involved flying aircraft.
questions.explanation: Melody Danquah trained as a pilot. Her flying helped open a path for other women in aviation.
questions.misconception: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.

distractorMisconceptions.Joyce Bamford-Addo: Bamford-Addo served as Speaker of Parliament.

questions.stem: Read this name card: “Elizabeth Ohene, editor of the Daily Graphic”. Copy the name of the editor.
hints: Find the person's name before the job.
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Ohene edited the Daily Graphic. An editor helps decide how news is prepared for readers.
questions.misconception: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.

questions.stem: Tell a partner who Georgina Wood was and name the place where a judge hears cases.
hints: Look for the job connected with courts.
questions.explanation: Georgina Wood became Ghana's first woman Chief Justice. Judges hear cases in courts.
questions.misconception: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.

criteria.description: Identifies Wood as Chief Justice.
Names courts as the setting for a judge's work.

questions.stem: Make a picture card to help a younger pupil remember Melody Danquah. Explain the picture you chose.
hints: Think of an object she learned to operate.
questions.explanation: An aircraft beside her name can remind the pupil that Melody Danquah flew as a pilot.
questions.misconception: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.

criteria.description: Links the card to Melody Danquah.
Makes and explains a picture connected with flying.

questions.stem: A display has swapped the labels “pilot” and “editor” under Elizabeth Ohene and Melody Danquah. Correct both labels and add a clue for one.
hints: Think about who worked with news and who worked with aircraft.
questions.explanation: Ohene belongs with editor and Danquah with pilot. A newspaper or an aircraft provides a useful clue.
questions.misconception: Similar titles and public roles can belong to different people.

criteria.description: Correctly restores both labels.
Adds an accurate clue for either woman's work.

questions.stem: Who became Ghana's first woman Speaker of Parliament?
hints: Think of the woman who guided meetings of Parliament.
questions.explanation: Joyce Bamford-Addo served as Speaker. The Speaker guides Parliament's meetings.
questions.misconception: The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.

distractorMisconceptions.Georgina Wood: Wood was the first woman Chief Justice.
distractorMisconceptions.Elizabeth Ohene: Ohene is known for editing a newspaper.

questions.stem: Which caption belongs under a picture of Georgina Wood at the courts?
hints: Think of the office she held.
questions.explanation: Georgina Wood led Ghana's judiciary as Chief Justice. The other captions describe different jobs.
questions.misconception: The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.
options: A pilot in Ghana's Air Force

distractorMisconceptions.Editor of the Daily Graphic: This caption belongs to Elizabeth Ohene.
distractorMisconceptions.Ghana's first woman Speaker: This caption belongs to Joyce Bamford-Addo.

questions.stem: Make two name slips, “Wood” and “Bamford-Addo”. Give the first to the learner playing Chief Justice and the second to the learner playing Speaker. Say each full name.
hints: Think of one woman at the courts and the other leading Parliament’s meetings.
questions.explanation: Georgina Wood held the office of Chief Justice. Joyce Bamford-Addo held the office of Speaker.
questions.misconception: The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.

criteria.description: Places the two slips with the correct roles.
Gives each woman's full name.

questions.stem: A pupil thinks being Speaker means giving every speech in Parliament. Use Joyce Bamford-Addo’s role to explain what the title means.
hints: What does someone who guides a meeting do?
questions.explanation: As Speaker, Bamford-Addo guided the meetings of Parliament. Other members could speak in those meetings.
questions.misconception: The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.

criteria.description: Names Joyce Bamford-Addo and her office.
Explains that the Speaker guides meetings where other members also speak.

questions.stem: Your class wants one sentence on how both a Chief Justice and a Speaker can serve Ghana. Include an example of each.
hints: Name the women first. Then give one duty for each.
questions.explanation: Georgina Wood led the courts as Chief Justice. Joyce Bamford-Addo chaired meetings of Parliament as Speaker.
questions.misconception: The Speaker of Parliament and the Chief Justice have different duties.

criteria.description: Identifies Wood and gives an accurate duty.
Identifies Bamford-Addo and gives an accurate duty.

questions.stem: Which example describes work done by newspaper editor Elizabeth Ohene?
hints: Think about the work that reaches newspaper readers.
questions.explanation: An editor helps prepare news for publication. Ohene did this work at the Daily Graphic.
questions.misconception: A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.
options: Flying an aircraft to its destination

distractorMisconceptions.Leading Ghana's courts: That is the Chief Justice's role.

questions.stem: Complete the job title in “As a ___, Melody Danquah learned to fly an aircraft.”
hints: Use the word for a person at the controls of a plane.
questions.explanation: A pilot operates an aircraft. Danquah is remembered in Ghana for this work.
questions.misconception: A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.

questions.stem: Which sentence explains why Georgina Wood's achievement mattered to a girl who wanted to be a judge?
hints: Look for a reason linked to what Wood did.
questions.explanation: Holding the office showed the girl an example of a Ghanaian woman leading the country's courts.
questions.misconception: A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.
options: She showed how to chair Parliament.
She showed a woman could lead Ghana's courts.
She showed where to train as a pilot.
She showed how to edit a newspaper.

questions.stem: Tell how editing a newspaper can help a community. Name the Ghanaian editor you learned about.
hints: Think of how readers get news.
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Ohene helped prepare news for readers. News can help readers learn what is happening in their communities.
questions.misconception: A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.

criteria.description: Identifies Elizabeth Ohene.
Explains one way newspaper work can help people.

questions.stem: Choose one Ghanaian woman from the lesson. Introduce her to a visitor using her name, her work and one reason pupils remember her.
hints: Give one detail beyond the name of her job.
questions.explanation: A pupil might introduce Melody Danquah as an early woman pilot who showed other girls that women could fly aircraft.
questions.misconception: A person's name or job title alone does not explain their contribution.

criteria.description: Names a woman and correctly identifies her work.
Explains a contribution or reason to remember her.

questions.stem: Which question would help you find out how a woman helped your community?
hints: Think about her actions and the people affected.
questions.explanation: Asking about a change she helped make invites an example of her contribution.
questions.misconception: Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.
options: What did her bag look like?
What did she help people do?

distractorMisconceptions.Which colour does she like?: A favourite colour gives a preference rather than a contribution.
distractorMisconceptions.Which shoes did she wear?: Shoes alone do not tell how she helped.
distractorMisconceptions.What did her bag look like?: A bag's appearance does not show her work.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to read Elizabeth Ohene's work. On a card marked “Daily Graphic newspaper”, which two words are the name of the paper?
hints: Look for the title before the word newspaper.
questions.explanation: Daily Graphic is the name of the newspaper that Ohene edited.
questions.misconception: Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.

questions.stem: Name a woman from your community or this lesson whose work you admire. Say what she did.
hints: Choose a concrete action that someone could describe.
questions.explanation: A learner could name a nurse who helps children at a clinic or Georgina Wood, who led Ghana’s courts.
questions.misconception: Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.

criteria.description: Identifies a woman by name or a clear local description.
Describes her work accurately.

questions.stem: Draw two panels to show a Ghanaian woman doing her work and someone helped by it. Explain how the pictures connect.
hints: Choose a woman you learned about or know in your community.
questions.explanation: One panel might show a local teacher helping a learner read. The other could show the learner reading a story.
questions.misconception: Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.

criteria.description: Shows or describes the work of an identifiable woman.
Connects that work to a credible benefit.

questions.stem: One pupil says, “I admire her.” Another asks, “Why?” Answer using something a Ghanaian woman did and a way you could learn from her.
hints: Link her action with a small action you could try.
questions.explanation: A pupil who admires editor Elizabeth Ohene might practise checking a class news report before sharing it.
questions.misconception: Fame or appearance alone does not explain how a person has helped a community.

criteria.description: Supports admiration with an accurate example of the woman's work.
Links the example to a realistic action the learner could take.

uncertain: Printed page 12 uses B2.2.5.1.1 in its content-standard column and places a full stop after the same code in the indicator column.

indicator.subject: History
indicator.content_standard: B2.3.2.1. Understand that trade was the major reason why the Europeans settled in Ghana
indicator.objective: Describe how early trade was carried out between Ghanaians and Europeans

skills.description: Explain a direct exchange of goods.
Recognise goods in the curriculum and describe their movement.
Connect coastal meeting places with trade by sea.
Use a story, objects or a role-play to explain how early trade worked.

spec.difficultyPlan: 5 recall, 7 simple use, 5 application and 3 challenge questions.
misconceptions: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.
Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.
Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.
A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

questions.stem: What is barter?
hints: Think of the items that change hands.
questions.explanation: In barter each trader gives goods and receives other goods in return.
questions.misconception: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.

distractorMisconceptions.Giving a friend a gift: A gift does not require goods in return.
distractorMisconceptions.Keeping goods for later: Keeping goods does not exchange them.
distractorMisconceptions.Borrowing goods for a day: Borrowed goods are meant to be returned.

questions.stem: Kojo and Efua swap a cloth card for a gold card, with no money. What kind of trade are they acting out?
hints: Use the name for swapping one good for another.
questions.explanation: Each gives one good to receive the other. Their card game represents barter.
questions.misconception: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.

questions.stem: One child gives cloth and receives an iron bar. Describe the swap from the other child's side.
hints: Exchange the words gives and receives as you change sides.
questions.explanation: The other child gives the iron bar and receives cloth. Both children can describe the same trade.
questions.misconception: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.

criteria.description: Names what the second child gives.
Names what the second child receives.

questions.stem: Take turns as traders. Use paper pictures of two goods to show a barter. Tell the class when the exchange is complete.
hints: Watch what each trader holds before and after.
questions.explanation: Once the partners agree, each gives their picture to receive the other one. Both goods have changed hands.
questions.misconception: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.

criteria.description: Shows an agreed two-way exchange with pictures.
Explains how each trader's goods changed.

questions.stem: A child says handing over an iron card is already barter. What more must you know? Give an example that is barter.
hints: Think about what the child gets back.
questions.explanation: Ask whether the child received another good in return. Trading the iron card for a cloth card would be barter.
questions.misconception: Giving a gift or borrowing an item differs from swapping goods.

criteria.description: Identifies the missing information about goods in return.
Gives an example of a two-way exchange of goods.

questions.stem: Which pair names goods on our early-trade list?
hints: Look for things a trader could carry or exchange from the lesson.
questions.explanation: Textiles and iron bars both appear in the examples of goods. The other pairs belong to a modern classroom or shop.
questions.misconception: Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.

distractorMisconceptions.Notebooks and markers: These classroom supplies are not the pair on the lesson list.

questions.stem: A trader's basket contains folded textiles. What are the textiles?
hints: Think of something a tailor might cut and sew.
questions.explanation: Textiles are cloth or fabric. They are among the goods named in the trade lesson.
questions.misconception: Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.

distractorMisconceptions.Pieces of gold: Gold is a separate trade item.

questions.stem: Make a picture key for two goods from the early-trade lesson. Show how a reader can tell your symbols apart.
hints: Choose goods with different shapes or textures.
questions.explanation: One drawing might show a folded cloth, the other a long iron bar. Writing or saying their names makes the symbols clear.
questions.misconception: Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.

criteria.description: Represents two goods named in the curriculum.
Labels or describes the two symbols clearly.

questions.stem: A trade story says the visiting trader gives textiles and receives gold. Put a paper label on each end of an arrow that shows where the textiles go.
hints: Follow the cloth, not the gold.
questions.explanation: The textiles move from the visiting trader to the local trader. Gold moves back the other way in this example.
questions.misconception: Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.

criteria.description: Places both traders at the correct ends of the textiles arrow.
Explains what went in the other direction.

questions.stem: A list names iron bars and gold but gives no names of traders. Can you tell who gave the gold in that particular swap? What would help?
hints: A list of things is different from a story about who did what.
questions.explanation: Either name could appear in a list without telling who gave it. A caption saying who handed the gold to whom would answer the question.
questions.misconception: Seeing an item on a trade list alone does not tell who gave it in a particular exchange.

criteria.description: Explains why the list cannot settle the direction of this swap.
Identifies a missing detail that would settle it.

questions.stem: Where does a ship meet traders who bring goods down to the sea?
hints: Think about the part of the land that touches the sea.
questions.explanation: Ships can reach a landing place on the coast. Traders can meet there with goods.
questions.misconception: Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.

distractorMisconceptions.At a hilltop: A ship at sea cannot reach the top of a hill.
distractorMisconceptions.At an inland field: An inland field does not meet the sea.
distractorMisconceptions.At a forest clearing inland: An inland clearing does not meet the sea.

questions.stem: Complete the class caption with one word from “coast” and “field”: traders welcomed a ship at the ___.
hints: Use the word for land beside the sea.
questions.explanation: The coast is where land meets the sea. A ship can bring goods to a landing place there.
questions.misconception: Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.

questions.stem: On a trade map, cloth travels by ship, then is carried to a market. What does the ship do in this story?
hints: Track the first part of the trip.
questions.explanation: The ship moves cloth across the water to a coastal meeting place. People can then carry it onwards.
questions.misconception: Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.
options: Weaves the cloth at the market
Makes the iron at the market

distractorMisconceptions.Weaves the cloth at the market: Weavers make cloth, and this trip starts after the cloth is made.
distractorMisconceptions.Makes the iron at the market: There is no iron-making step in this story.
distractorMisconceptions.Chooses what all buyers want: A ship carries goods and cannot make that choice.

questions.stem: Draw a ship, a shore and a market in a town. Use arrows to show how a piece of cloth could reach a buyer there.
hints: Begin where the cloth is carried across water.
questions.explanation: An arrow can lead from ship to shore and another from shore to market. Together they show the cloth's route.
questions.misconception: Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.

criteria.description: Places the ship, shore and market in a sensible order.
Uses arrows or a spoken explanation to trace the cloth to a buyer.

questions.stem: Long ago a small coastal town had a landing place. More traders started coming there. Explain one way the trade could change the town.
hints: What might the visitors need a place for?
questions.explanation: People might sell more goods or make room to keep them near the landing place. The town could grow around that trade.
questions.misconception: Trade can help a town grow even when people already live there.

criteria.description: Identifies a plausible change connected with more trade.
Explains how the traders' needs could lead to the change.

questions.stem: Which question would help you complete the story “a trader offered cloth”?
hints: Find out about the other side of the trade.
questions.explanation: Asking what the trader received tells whether and how an exchange happened.
questions.misconception: A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

distractorMisconceptions.What colour was the sky?: Sky colour does not tell what was exchanged.
distractorMisconceptions.How tall was the trader?: Height does not describe the exchange.
distractorMisconceptions.How large was the cloud?: Cloud size does not identify the goods received.

questions.stem: A play has a card reading “the visiting trader receives an iron bar”. What item should that trader hold at the end?
hints: Read the words after receives.
questions.explanation: At the end of this example, the visiting trader has the iron bar. The card says who received it.
questions.misconception: A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

questions.stem: Pretend you watched a local trader and a European trader swapping picture cards. Tell what they each had at the start.
hints: Choose one good for each person from the lesson.
questions.explanation: You might say the local trader had a gold card and the visitor had a cloth card. This prepares a listener to follow the exchange.
questions.misconception: A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

criteria.description: Identifies both traders in the example.
Assigns one appropriate good to each at the start.

questions.stem: Show a partner two scenes with cards. In the first, trade cloth for an iron bar. In the second, buy the cloth with money. Explain the change.
hints: Watch what is given in return for the cloth.
questions.explanation: The first scene uses goods on both sides. In the second scene the buyer gives money for the cloth.
questions.misconception: A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

criteria.description: Demonstrates barter in the first scene and a purchase in the second.
Identifies the change in what was given for the cloth.

questions.stem: Write or dictate a tiny play about an early trade at the coast. Give both traders a line and tell how the goods change hands.
hints: Let each trader say what they offer or want.
questions.explanation: One trader might offer gold for cloth. The other can agree and hand over cloth in return for gold. Both lines help the audience follow the swap.
questions.misconception: A clear account includes both parties and what each exchanged.

criteria.description: Gives a suitable part to each trader in a coastal setting.
Describes which goods each trader gives or receives.

uncertain: Printed page 13 lists trade goods together without consistently identifying their direction. The questions specify who gives each item in illustrative exchanges.
